learning_objective: 🎯 Understand the 'Central Dogma of Molecular Biology'—how the code of life is copied, read, and translated into the proteins that make you, you!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Proposed by Francis Crick, it states that genetic information flows in one direction: DNA -> RNA -> Protein. (Exception: Retroviruses like HIV do reverse transcription: RNA -> DNA).
The process where DNA makes an exact copy of itself before cell division. It is 'semi-conservative', meaning each new DNA molecule has one old strand and one newly synthesized strand.
The process of copying a gene's DNA sequence into messenger RNA (mRNA). The enzyme RNA Polymerase opens the DNA and builds the RNA strand.
Occurs in the ribosomes. The mRNA is read in sets of three bases (codons). Transfer RNA (tRNA) brings the matching amino acids to build a protein chain.
Cells don't need all proteins all the time. Gene regulation (like the lac operon in bacteria) acts as an on/off switch to ensure proteins are only made when needed.

fun_activity.title: 🔢 The Codon Decoder
fun_activity.instructions: If DNA is TAC-CGA-TTC, the mRNA will be AUG-GCU-AAG (remember, RNA uses U instead of T). Write your own short 9-letter DNA sequence and translate it into mRNA!

exam_tips: 📌 Always remember directionality: DNA replication and RNA transcription ALWAYS occur in the 5' to 3' direction.
📌 Know the difference between the 'template strand' (which RNA polymerase reads) and the 'coding strand' (which has the exact same sequence as the new RNA, except T is replaced by U).
📌 The start codon is AUG, which codes for Methionine. There are 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) that do not code for any amino acids.
quick_recap: ⭐ Helicase unzips DNA, DNA Polymerase builds the new strand, and Ligase glues the fragments together.
⭐ Eukaryotic mRNA requires processing (splicing to remove introns, adding a 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail) before it leaves the nucleus.
⭐ The genetic code is universal; the same codons code for the same amino acids in almost all living organisms.
